report.source_text: On March 11, 2011, the patient witnessed his wife being swept away in front of him by the tsunami resulting from the Great East Japan Earthquake. Following the accident at the FDNPP, he evacuated with his family and returned to his hometown 1 year later. For 2 years after returning to his hometown, he lived with his father and his son’s family while taking care of his father. After living with his son’s family for more than 1 year after placing his father in a nursing home, he began to frequently lose valuable items. He began to suspect that his son had stolen them, and this issue eventually caused the son and his family to move out.

report.source_text: During the first visit, the patient had no serious feelings about his memory loss. He went out almost every day to interact with his acquaintances and returned home without getting lost, but he could not report how he spent the day. He was able to contact his friends using his mobile phone and drove on his own without any trouble or traffic violations. He denied having any depressive feelings, and no obvious weight loss was observed. When we asked if he got lost when he went out, he gave an unrelated answer: “I’m going to see the sea.” He was also able to recount in detail how his wife was swept away by the tsunami. During testing, the patient scored 16 on the Revised Hasegawa Dementia Scale (HDS-R), indicating a decline in cognitive function.

report.source_text: Because the patient’s relationship with his son was strained, we had nurses and support service providers assist the patient with daily tasks (e.g. cooking, cleaning, and taking medicine). Before beginning treatment, the patient spent the entirety of every day outside of the house and was unable to turn off the lights at night. We thought that he might be feeling anxious or nervous and began treating him with sertraline (25 mg daily) in May 20XX+1. Very quickly, he began to spend less time outside, started turning off the lights when going to sleep, and was able to remain calm while speaking about his wife. He would also sometimes spend time at senior care facility and began to look forward to the activities planned there.

He said that he could remember better than before.

Clinical presentation shows selective memory loss (cannot recall daily activities but can drive, use phone, recount traumatic event in detail) with lack of concern and preserved functional abilities—more consistent with dissociative amnesia than progressive neurodegeneration. WAIS-III showed normal IQ ranges (81 full-scale, 80 verbal, 87 performance). After sertraline treatment began in May 20XX+1, the patient showed rapid behavioral improvement: decreased time outside, began turning off lights, remained calm discussing wife, and engaged in senior care activities. At 100 mg/day sertraline in June 20XX+1, he developed drug-induced hypomania (extravagant spending), requiring termination after 3 months. After stopping sertraline, his tendency to frequently leave the house did not return, and he reported improved memory. This clinical trajectory—selective memory loss, preserved function, rapid response to SSRI with behavioral improvement, and memory improvement after medication discontinuation—supports dissociative disorder diagnosis rather than progressive neurodegenerative disease.

report.source_text: The patient was housed in a residential complex constructed for evacuees from the nuclear disaster at Fukushima, and he began to actively interact with others who were in similar circumstances. He was tenderly cared for by the other residents of this community, and his memory impairment improved gradually. Approximately 9 months after discharge, although delayed recall was at 2 points, the total MMSE score improved to 26, which is within the normal range (Table 1).

clinician.final_diagnosis: Dissociative disorder secondary to psychological trauma (continuing dissociation resulting in memory impairment)
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 69-year-old male presented with severe memory impairment 1 year after separation from his son's family. He had experienced cumulative psychological trauma: witnessing his wife swept away by the 2011 tsunami, nuclear evacuation stress, and family separation after conflict with his son over suspected theft. Initially diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease based on HDS-R score of 16 and CT findings of suspected right lateral ventricle dilatation. However, clinical features were atypical for Alzheimer's: selective memory loss (unable to recall daily activities but able to drive, use mobile phone, recount traumatic event in detail), lack of concern about memory loss, and preserved functional abilities. WAIS-III showed normal IQ ranges (81 full-scale, 80 verbal, 87 performance). Sertraline treatment (25-100 mg/day) initiated in May 20XX+1 produced rapid behavioral improvement (decreased time outside, began turning off lights, remained calm discussing wife, engaged in senior care activities), suggesting anxiety-related dissociative symptoms rather than neurodegenerative disease. At 100 mg/day, drug-induced hypomania developed (extravagant spending), requiring termination after 3 months. After stopping sertraline, the tendency to frequently leave the house did not return and patient reported improved memory. Approximately 9 months after discharge, when housed in a residential complex for nuclear evacuees with tender care and social support from others in similar circumstances, MMSE score improved to 26 (within normal range) and memory impairment improved gradually. The clinical course—selective memory loss, preserved function, rapid response to SSRI, memory improvement after medication discontinuation, and gradual improvement with social support—supports dissociative disorder diagnosis rather than progressive neurodegenerative disease.
